title: reserved-gpu-commitment-playbook-sla-isolation
content:
Executive summary:

This playbook is a sales-and-procurement-facing brief that frames Redwood Dedicated (reserved GPU pools) as the procurement-friendly option for customers that require isolation, deterministic throughput, and contractual SLAs. It is intended for AE/SE use during procurement cycles and for Solutions to prepare RFP responses.

Goal: give the field a repeatable narrative, negotiation levers, a procurement checklist, and competitive talking points to win committed capacity deals with predictable unit economics and enterprise-ready controls.

Key themes (one-liners):
- Deterministic throughput: reserved capacity guarantees baseline throughput (tokens/sec, concurrent sessions) so product SLAs don't fluctuate with noisy neighbors.
- Contracted reliability: SLA-backed uptime and latency targets with service credits and measured SLO reporting.
- Data isolation & compliance: private tenancy, VPC peering or on-prem options, and integrations with customer KMS for key custody.
- Cost predictability: committed monthly/annual pricing with smoothing and rollover options, and tooling to measure unit cost per request.

Target buyers / personas:
- Platform / Infrastructure lead (platform team): cares about predictable QoS and developer standardization across teams.
- Head of ML/ML infra: needs throughput guarantees for production inference and model rollout predictability.
- Procurement & Legal: contracting cadence, payment terms, SLAs, termination, and exit assistance.
- Security/ Compliance Officer: needs proof of isolation, audit logs, SOC2, and KMS/HSM integration.

SLA & performance positioning (recommended wording for proposals):
- Availability: 99.9% uptime for Dedicated clusters (measured at the cluster level, excluding scheduled maintenance with at least 72 hours' notice).
- Latency: P99 per-token latency target of X ms for configured model families under the committed concurrency envelope (define per-customer profile during scoping).
- Throughput guarantee: baseline throughput commitments expressed as "concurrent inference units" or "tokens/sec" with documented burst policies and a documented degradation ladder if underlying hardware faults occur.
- Credits: service credits on missed SLA tiers, capped in total liability (see standard redwood enterprise T&Cs).

How isolation is implemented and why it matters (talking points for technical evaluators):
- Dedicated GPUs and tenant isolation: customers get dedicated GPU pools logically isolated from other tenants to eliminate noisy neighbor interference.
- Network model: VPC peering or private interconnect; optional air-gapped on-prem appliance for regulated data flows.
- Key management: customer-provided KMS/HSM for encryption keys at rest and in transit; logs are delivered to customer SIEM via secure forwarding.
- Audit & compliance: per-request audit logs, retention controls, and support for enterprise export formats.

Predictable throughput: product controls and configuration to emphasize in scoping:
- Capacity sizing: we sell in reserved units (e.g., n x GPU slots) with standard throughput benchmarks per model class. Sizing plan includes buffer for peak bursts and autoscale headroom.
- Autoscale/overflow policy: reserved capacity + controlled burst into shared pool for short spikes (optional); customers can opt out of shared-burst behavior for stricter isolation.
- QoS tiers: tiered routing (dedicated -> regional -> fallback model family) to maintain uptime while capping cost. Include documented fallback models and functional equivalence metrics.
- Monitoring & Ops: per-route dashboards, tracing, and token-level cost/latency breakdowns exposed in the Redwood Console for chargeback and capacity planning.

Procurement-playbook: steps and artifacts to hand to procurement/legal
1) Discovery & scoping: gather API QPS, model families, peak token/sec, regulatory constraints, desired RTO/RPO. Use our sizing template (linked in artifacts).
2) Sizing & proposal: propose reserved units, burst policy, and monitoring add-ons; include benchmark attachments for representative models.
3) Contract & SLA: propose term (12/24/36 months), renewal mechanics, service credits matrix, and termination assistance clause (data export + air-gapped handover).
4) Security review: provide SOC2 report, architecture diagram, list of third-party subprocessors, KMS integration guide.
5) Procurement handoff: include an itemized bill-of-materials (reserved slots, console seats, premium support, observability retention, professional services for migration).

Procurement negotiation levers (what field can offer week-to-week):
- Price flexibility: month-to-month vs 12/24/36 mo commitments, stepped discounts for longer commitments or higher units.
- Payment terms: Net-30/Net-60; prepaid annual discounts.
- Onboarding credits: free migration support hours or limited free professional services to justify switch.
- SLO customization: raise per-customer P99/throughput targets for an uplift in price or include dedicated engineering support.
- Exit assistance: data export and limited on-site/remote transfer support as a contractual add-on.

Competitive positioning (quick matrix and messaging):
- Against cloud-managed endpoints (AWS SageMaker endpoints, GCP Vertex AI endpoints):
  - Win: consistent, lower per-token cost at scale due to model-optimized runtime, and clearer high-throughput economics (reserved units).
  - Lose: cloud vendors offer deeper cloud integration or large enterprise discounts in some accounts — mitigate with joint-arch guidance and marketplace listings.
- Against self-hosting (in-house infra or vendors like Kube-based inference stacks):
  - Win: we run the model-serving optimizations, kernel selection and operational runbooks so customers avoid long ops cycles and cost of hiring specialized SRE/Inference engineers.
  - Lose: customers with existing infra investments may prefer self-hosting for full control — offer migration assistance and hybrid private deployment options.
- Against specialized inference vendors:
  - Win: Redwood provides unified experience across hosted/dedicated/private with strong developer UX, built-in observability, and procurement-ready SLAs.
  - Lose: smaller niche vendors may beat on single metric (latency best-case) — respond with real-world P99 metrics and production case studies.

Common objections & suggested rebuttals:
- Objection: "We can just run this ourselves on our GPUs"
  - Rebuttal: upfront infra and personnel costs, plus slower time-to-production and lack of ongoing kernel/optimizer investment. Offer TCO comparison (we can generate a tailored TCO for their QPS).
- Objection: "We need full physical isolation / air gap"
  - Rebuttal: we offer private/on-prem packages and an air-gapped deployment option with professional services; describe our data transfer and handover playbook.
- Objection: "SLA doesn't cover our latency requirements"
  - Rebuttal: SLAs are configurable at negotiation; we can build a performance profile and optionally commit higher P99 targets for a price uplift.

Procurement-ready attachments to include with proposals (checklist to attach to quote):
- Benchmarks for the requested model family (P50/P95/P99 tokens latency, throughput at 50/75/90 percentile concurrency).
- Capacity sizing worksheet and bill of materials.
- Security pack: SOC2 Type II, subprocessors, KMS integration doc, pen test summary.
- SLA & T&C summary (call out service credits, liability cap, maintenance window policy).
- Runbook excerpt: incident response, escalation matrix, data export and backup procedures.

Sample outreach snippets (use in email/slide intro):
- Email subject: "Proposal: Dedicated inference capacity & SLA to stabilize your product SLAs"
- Email body blurb: "We propose a reserved GPU pool sized for your peak inference needs with 99.9% uptime, P99 latency guarantees for the selected models, VPC-level isolation, and an enterprise-ready onboarding plan with migration credits. Attached: benchmarks, capacity worksheet, and security pack."

Playbook for AE/SE during scoping call (practical checklist):
- Confirm QPS, average prompt length, peak concurrency windows, and model families in use.
- Ask about regulatory constraints (data residency, encryption keys, air-gap needs).
- Clarify tolerance for degraded models vs total outage during hardware failures.
- Determine procurement timeline and preferred term (start/end dates).
- Ask for procurement contacts and security review cadence; set expectations on artefacts turnaround time.

Open risks and mitigations (internal notes):
- Risk: Under-sizing leads to frequent burst into shared pool and unhappy customer.
  - Mitigation: conservative buffer in the first 90 days and a capacity review at 30/60/90 days.
- Risk: Legal pushes back on liability cap / data residency language.
  - Mitigation: pre-approved legal templates and a standard limited-data residency addendum.
- Risk: Customer expects per-request latency parity with best-case microbenchmarks.
  - Mitigation: share production-like benchmarking methodology and require a short proof-of-concept run.

Next steps & owner action items:
